§9.8.1 Rotated and Diagonal Content

📄 Page rule — applied from the page alone

tables-rotated-and-diagonal-content · tables orientation headers

✅ Normative

A rotated table MUST be read in its own orientation, never in page orientation. A diagonally split corner cell MUST stay one cell holding both labels separated by a slash — Region \ Year — the label across the top first.

One printed cell carrying two labels: MONTH across the top, COUNTRY down the side, split by a diagonal rule. There is only one cell to put them in.

A landscape table on a portrait page

  • A table printed sideways MUST be rendered as a reader would read it after turning the page: rows are rows as the table reads, not as the page is filed.
  • Sideways text MUST NOT be transcribed in page order.

Vertical column headers

Labels printed at 90° over narrow columns are ordinary headers. Each MUST be rendered as normal header text, upright, in the column it heads.

| ⤴A⤴ | ⤴B⤴ | ⤴C⤴ |   ← headers printed vertically
| 1   | 2   | 3   |

Nothing about the rotation changes the structure — it is a typesetting choice made because the column is narrow.

The diagonally split corner cell

| Region ╲ Year | 2023 | 2024 |   ← one printed cell, two labels
| East          | 40   | 44   |
  • Both labels MUST survive: one names the stub column, the other names the header row, and losing either leaves an axis unnamed.
  • There is one printed cell, so it MUST stay one cell, the two labels separated by a slash — Region \ Year — in the reading order the diagonal implies: the label across the top first, then the one down the side.
  • The corner MUST NOT be split into two header cells.

✅ Sample — a landscape page in a portrait document

A paper page rendered sideways: the body text, both tables and the Table 3 caption read bottom-to-top. Upright, the two tables are ordinary tables; nothing about them is special except that a reader has to turn the page. The page is cut off after the Kestrel 33B row of the second table, so nothing below it is rendered.

What makes this the useful case is that the rotation is not marked anywhere. There is no landscape flag; the only signal is that the text runs the wrong way. A rendering in page orientation transposes headers and rows and still looks structurally plausible.

Note also the blank corner cells above both stub columns, and the en-dashes standing in for missing benchmark scores — see Barely-Existing Columns and Headers§9.3.1 and Marks and Symbols in Cells§9.6.6.

✅ Sample — a vertical stub header

The leftmost column carries a label running bottom-to-top along the side of the table, spanning every body row, while all the other headers sit horizontally. It labels the whole stub, which is why the typesetter turned it — there was no width for it any other way. The coloured shapes in the second column have no legend on the page, so each is described as drawn.

The rotation is a layout constraint, not a property of the header: the label is rendered upright as a normal header cell spanning the rows it spans. The table's bilingual text and its landscape setting change nothing either.

✅ Sample — a landscape reference table on a portrait page

Table C.1. (Cont.): twenty-five chemicals with CAS numbers, formulae and properties, printed sideways. Upright it is an ordinary eleven-column table (No. plus ten property columns); the header cells carry units and subscripts (D_a, cm² s⁻¹), the formulae carry subscripts, and one melting point prints 123.5 decomposes on two lines. The page number C-6, printed beside the title in the table's own orientation, is rendered first as the page's header band.
